name: Gatehouse Veil
geological_features: Layered cloud veils of varying opacity
specific_features: A gap in the inner cloud layer that permits direct observation of the deep atmosphere -- the 'Gate'
description: Gatehouse Veil is a gas giant distinguished by its extraordinarily layered atmosphere, where multiple distinct cloud decks create a series of veils that obscure the planet's deeper layers. The outermost veil is a pale, translucent haze; beneath it, progressively denser and more colorful cloud bands alternate between opaque barriers and semi-transparent windows. A persistent gap in the inner cloud layer -- the Gate -- permits rare direct observation of the deep atmosphere, revealing swirling patterns of vivid crimson and indigo.

The planet's chromophore-rich cloud bands produce a color palette more varied than most gas giants, ranging from sulfurous yellow through deep burgundy to near-black. Anticyclonic ovals drift through the middle cloud layers, their rotation creating temporary clearings in the veils above. The effect is one of a world constantly revealing and concealing itself, its deeper nature glimpsed only through fleeting apertures in its atmospheric defenses.

The Gate phenomenon has been the subject of extensive study, as no satisfactory model explains why this particular region of the inner cloud deck remains permanently clear while surrounding areas maintain dense coverage. Atmospheric probes sent through the Gate have transmitted data from depths rarely accessible on gas giants, revealing an ammonia ocean at the liquid-gas boundary and complex organic chemistry in the transition zone.

Gatehouse Veil's scientific value is considerable -- the Gate provides a natural observatory into gas giant deep-atmosphere processes that would otherwise require prohibitively expensive penetration missions. Research stations maintain permanent orbits aligned with the Gate, their instruments trained on the narrow window into the planet's interior. The fuel reserves in the upper atmosphere are accessible but secondary to the planet's primary role as a natural laboratory for atmospheric science.
